title: Numbers & Counting
description: Number sense grows from counting real things to understanding place value, fractions, negative numbers and the number system itself. Every stage connects symbols to quantities and asks children to explain how they know.

stages.overview: Counting real objects to 10, recognising numerals, and comparing small groups.
goals: Count up to 10 objects, touching each one once
Say which group has more or fewer

lessons.title: Touch and Count
objectives: Count up to 10 objects by touching each one once
Understand that the last number said tells how many there are
prerequisites: Can say the numbers 1 to 5 in order
explanation: When we count, we say one number for each thing. We touch or move each thing as we say its number, so nothing is counted twice and nothing is missed.
The last number we say tells us how many there are altogether. If we count "1, 2, 3" for three bananas, there are 3 bananas — even if we count them in a different order.
Moving things into a "counted" pile is a great trick. Things that have been counted go on one side; things still to count stay on the other.

vocabulary.meaning: say numbers in order, one for each thing
the total number of things
all of them together
a group of things put together

examples: Counting stairs: say one number for each step you climb.
Counting spoons when setting the table: one spoon for each person, 1, 2, 3, 4.

story.title: Kiko Counts the Mangoes
story.text: Kiko the mountain goat found mangoes under a tree. "One, two, two, three!" Kiko said, touching one mango twice. Olu the owl laughed kindly. "Let's move each mango into the basket as we count." Kiko tried again: "One… two… three… four!" Four mangoes went into the basket, one at a time. "The last number is four, so there are four mangoes," said Kiko proudly.

activities.why: Touch each apple: 1, 2, 3, 4. The last number is 4.

activities.prompt: Kiko counted 🍌🍌🍌 as "1, 2, 3". How many bananas?
activities.why: The last number counted tells how many.

activities.prompt: Put the numbers in counting order

thinking: If you count the same toys starting from the other end, will you get a different number? Why?
Why is it a good idea to move toys when you count them?
speaking: Count your fingers on one hand out loud and tell a grown-up how many there are.
Explain to someone how you make sure you never count a toy twice.

Match a numeral to a group with that many things

lessons.title: Which Number Is This?
objectives: Recognise the written numerals 0 to 10
Match a numeral to a group with that many things
explanation: Numbers have shapes that we write down. The shape "3" means three things, like three birds or three claps. Each number shape is called a numeral.
Zero, written 0, means none at all. An empty plate has zero cookies. Zero is still a number — it tells us there is nothing there.
When you see a numeral, you can show it with fingers, claps or objects. When you see a group, you can find the numeral that matches it.

vocabulary.meaning: the written shape of a number, like 5
none at all, written 0
find two things that go together

examples: A house number on a door, like 7, tells which house it is.
Lift buttons show numerals for each floor.

story.title: The Empty Nest
story.text: Mayur the peacock peeked into a nest. "How many eggs?" asked Tara the tortoise. "None! The birds have hatched and flown away," said Mayur. "So the number is zero," smiled Tara, and she drew a round 0 in the sand. "Zero means nothing is there."

activities.prompt: Match the number to the group
An empty plate has how many cookies?
Show the numeral as a count: how many dots? ● ● ● ● ● ● ●

thinking: Is zero a number even though there is nothing there? What do you think?
Where do you see numerals around your home?
speaking: Go on a numeral hunt and tell a grown-up three numbers you found and where.

project.title: Numeral Hunt Poster

Next to each one, draw or stick that many things
Read your poster aloud to a family member

mastery: Names numerals 0–10 shown in random order
Matches numerals to sets correctly for 0–10
Explains what zero means using an example

units.summary: Comparing two groups by matching and counting.
objectives: Compare two groups and say which has more or fewer
Use matching (pairing up) to compare without counting
masteryCriteria: Compares groups up to 10 correctly using matching or counting
Uses the words more, fewer and same correctly
Explains that bigger objects do not mean a bigger number

revision.notes: Revisit through play: replay one activity, retell the story, and do one hands-on task. Keep revision under 5 minutes.

lessons.title: Which Group Has More?
objectives: Compare two groups and say which has more or fewer
Use matching (pairing up) to compare without counting
explanation: To find which group has more, we can pair things up: one from this group with one from that group. The group with things left over has more.
We can also count both groups. The bigger number means more things. If both numbers are the same, the groups are equal.
Big things do not always mean more! Three elephants and three ants are the same number, even though elephants are much bigger.

vocabulary.meaning: a bigger number of things
a smaller number of things
equal, not more and not fewer
two things put together

examples: Four children and three chairs: one child has no chair, so there are more children than chairs.
Three elephants and three ants: the same number of animals.

story.title: Chairs for the Party
story.text: Momo the bear invited friends for tea. Five friends came, but there were only four chairs. Everyone sat down, and Zuri the zebra was left standing. "We have more friends than chairs!" said Momo, and fetched one more chair. Now every friend had exactly one chair — the same number.

activities.why: Pair them up: two strawberries are left over in the group of 5.

activities.prompt: 🐘🐘🐘 and 🐜🐜🐜 have the same number of animals.
activities.why: Size does not change the number.

activities.prompt: Put these from fewest to most

thinking: If you have 3 big cookies and a friend has 4 small cookies, who has more cookies? Who has more to eat?
How could you check who has more without counting?
speaking: Make two piles of toys and tell a grown-up which pile has more and how you know.

project.title: Cups and Spoons Matching Game

Put one spoon in each cup
See whether there are spoons or cups left over
Say "more spoons", "more cups" or "the same"

stages.overview: Counting to 20 and beyond, counting on, and seeing numbers as made of smaller parts.
goals: Count, read and write numbers to 20

units.title: Numbers to 20
units.summary: Teen numbers are "ten and some more".
objectives: Read and count numbers from 11 to 20
Explain that teen numbers are made of one ten and some ones
masteryCriteria: Counts objects to 20 accurately
Describes any teen number as ten and some ones
Places numbers 0–20 in order

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: Ten and Some More
objectives: Read and count numbers from 11 to 20
Explain that teen numbers are made of one ten and some ones
explanation: Numbers from 11 to 19 are called teen numbers. Each one is made of a full ten and some more ones. Fourteen is ten and four more.
We write teen numbers with two digits. In 14, the 1 stands for one ten and the 4 stands for four ones. That is why fourteen starts with a 1.
Twenty is two tens. When we count past 19, we fill a second ten and start a new pattern: 20, 21, 22.

vocabulary.meaning: the numbers 13 to 19 (and 11, 12, made the same way)
one of the symbols 0–9 used to write numbers
a box of 10 spaces for counting

examples: Two hands of fingers (10) plus three more fingers from a friend makes 13.
A full egg carton of 10 eggs plus 2 more eggs is 12 eggs.

story.title: The Ten-Bead Necklace
story.text: Rangi the chameleon made a necklace with exactly ten blue beads. Then Rangi added six red beads. "How many beads now?" asked Bolt the robot. Rangi said, "Ten blue… and eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen red. Sixteen! Ten and six more."

activities.prompt: Ten frame full (10) plus ●●● — how many?

thinking: Why do you think we say "fourteen" and not "ten-four"?
Is 17 closer to 10 or to 20? How do you know?
speaking: Show a teen number with your fingers and a friend's fingers, and explain the ten and the ones.

project.title: Teen Number Egg Cartons
materials: two egg cartons (or drawn ten frames)
steps: Fill one carton completely with 10 objects
Put some objects in the second carton
Count the total starting from ten
Write the number and say "ten and ___ more"

assessment.prompt: Which number is ten and seven?

mastery: Counts objects to 20 accurately
Describes any teen number as ten and some ones
Places numbers 0–20 in order

units.title: Number Bonds to 10
units.summary: Numbers can be split into parts and put back together.
objectives: Find pairs of numbers that make 10
Use a part-part-whole picture to show a number bond
masteryCriteria: Recalls all bonds to 10 within a few seconds

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: Make Ten
objectives: Find pairs of numbers that make 10
Use a part-part-whole picture to show a number bond
explanation: A number can be split into two parts. Ten can be 7 and 3, or 6 and 4. The parts together make the whole. This is called a number bond.
Fingers are a helpful tool: hold up 10 fingers, fold some down, and the folded and standing fingers are the two parts.
Knowing bonds to 10 by heart makes adding and subtracting faster later, because 10 is the building block of our number system.

vocabulary.meaning: the total amount
one piece of the whole
two parts that make a whole

examples: 10 crayons: 4 in the box and 6 on the table.
10 fingers: 8 standing up and 2 folded down.

story.title: Ten Little Fish
story.text: Pala the dolphin was looking after ten little fish. Some hid behind a rock. Pala could see seven. "Three must be hiding," Pala thought, "because seven and three make ten." Pala swam behind the rock — and there they were, three little fish!

activities.prompt: 10 fish. You can see 🐟🐟🐟🐟🐟🐟. How many are hiding?

thinking: How many different ways can you make 10 with two numbers?
If you know 3 and 7 make 10, what else do you know?
speaking: Use your fingers to show a grown-up three ways to make 10, and say each one out loud.

project.title: Shake and Spill
steps: Put 10 counters in a cup and shake
Spill them out
Count how many show each colour
Record the bond like 6 + 4
Repeat and find all the different bonds

assessment.prompt: 10 birds. 8 flew away. How many are left?

mastery: Recalls all bonds to 10 within a few seconds
Finds a missing part of 10 without counting all
Explains number bonds with a picture or objects

Explains the role of zero as a place holder

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: Bundles of Ten
objectives: Explain the value of each digit in a two-digit number
Partition a number into tens and ones (47 = 40 + 7)
prerequisites: Understands teen numbers as ten and some ones
explanation: Counting large groups is easier if we bundle things into tens. Thirty-four sticks can be 3 bundles of ten and 4 loose sticks.
In a two-digit number, the left digit tells how many tens and the right digit tells how many ones. In 34, the 3 means 3 tens (thirty) and the 4 means 4 ones.
The same digit can have different values: the 5 in 52 is worth fifty, but the 5 in 25 is worth only five. This is place value.

vocabulary.meaning: the value a digit has because of its place
groups of ten
single units
split a number into parts

examples: 47 = 4 tens and 7 ones = 40 + 7.
Ten-rupee notes and one-rupee coins: 3 notes and 6 coins is ₹36.

story.title: The Stick Bundle Market
story.text: At the market, Zuri sold sticks for building. Customers kept asking, "How many sticks?" Counting one by one took ages. So Zuri tied the sticks into bundles of ten. "Fifty-three, please," said Kiko. Zuri handed over five bundles and three loose sticks in seconds.

activities.prompt: 3 bundles of ten and 5 loose sticks make…
In 25 and 52, the digit 5 has the same value.
activities.why: In 25 it is 5 ones; in 52 it is 5 tens, or fifty.

thinking: Why do you think people chose to group in tens?
What would happen if we had no zero? How would we write 30?
speaking: Explain to a family member why 52 and 25 are different numbers even though they use the same digits.

project.title: Straw Bundle Bank

Bundle every ten with a rubber band
Write the number as tens and ones
Draw it as a picture of bundles and singles

mastery: Identifies the value of each digit in any two-digit number
Partitions two-digit numbers into tens and ones in more than one way (e.g. 47 = 30 + 17)
Explains the role of zero as a place holder

units.summary: Numbers that pair up, and symbols for comparing.
objectives: Decide whether a number is odd or even by pairing
Use <, > and = to compare two-digit numbers
masteryCriteria: Classifies numbers to 100 as odd or even and justifies with pairing
Compares two-digit numbers correctly with <, >, =
Explains the strategy of comparing tens first

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: Odd or Even?
objectives: Decide whether a number is odd or even by pairing
Use <, > and = to compare two-digit numbers
explanation: If every object in a group can be put into pairs with none left over, the number is even. If one is left over, the number is odd.
You only need to look at the ones digit: numbers ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 are even; numbers ending in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 are odd.
To compare two numbers, compare the tens first. 41 > 39 because 4 tens is more than 3 tens. If the tens are equal, compare the ones. The symbol always opens toward the bigger number.

vocabulary.meaning: can be split into pairs with none left over
one left over after pairing
bigger than
smaller than

examples: Socks come in pairs, so a full sock drawer has an even number of socks.
56 > 52 because the tens are the same and 6 ones is more than 2 ones.

story.title: The Dance Partners
story.text: At the Heart Harbor dance, everyone needed a partner. Fourteen animals arrived and made seven pairs. Then Momo the bear arrived — fifteen! One left over. "Fifteen is odd," said Rangi, "so I'll dance with Momo and we'll make a group of three!"

activities.why: Pair 7 things: one is left over.

activities.prompt: Match each number to the right description

thinking: Is zero odd or even? Use the pairing idea to decide.
If you add two odd numbers, is the answer odd or even? Try some and look for a pattern.
speaking: Teach a grown-up the "look at the last digit" trick for odd and even, and prove it with objects.

project.title: Odd–Even Pairs Investigation

Describe the pattern you see

mastery: Classifies numbers to 100 as odd or even and justifies with pairing

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Rounding Numbers
objectives: Round numbers to the nearest 10 and 100
Use rounding to estimate and check answers
prerequisites: Can place numbers on a number line
explanation: Rounding means finding a nearby "friendly" number that is easier to work with. 47 rounds to 50 because on a number line 47 is closer to 50 than to 40.
Look at the digit to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 5 or more, round up; if it is 4 or less, round down. 350 rounded to the nearest 100 is 400 by this convention.
Rounding is used for estimating: 298 + 405 is about 300 + 400 = 700. If your exact answer is far from your estimate, check your work.

vocabulary.meaning: change a number to a nearby simpler number
a sensible approximate answer
closest
an agreed rule everyone uses

examples: A book costs ₹198 — about ₹200.
A crowd of 4,812 people is reported as "about 5,000".

story.title: The Quick Shopkeeper
story.text: Kiko bought three things costing ₹49, ₹31 and ₹78. "That's about 50 plus 30 plus 80 — around ₹160," Kiko said before the shopkeeper finished adding. The exact total was ₹158. "Your estimate was close, so my sum is probably right," said the shopkeeper.

activities.why: The tens digit is 5, so round up by convention.

thinking: When is it better to estimate than to calculate exactly? When is it not okay?
A news report says "about 2,000 people". Could the real number be 1,600? Why or why not?
speaking: Explain to someone how you would quickly check whether 389 + 412 = 701 is sensible.

project.title: Supermarket Estimate Challenge
materials: a grocery receipt or a pretend price list
steps: Round every price to the nearest 10
Add the rounded prices for an estimate
Add the exact prices
Compare and explain the difference

assessment.why: The tens digit is 4, so round down.

assessment.prompt: Estimating can help you spot a mistake.

mastery: Rounds any number to 10,000 to the nearest 10 and 100
Uses estimates to judge whether a calculated answer is reasonable
Explains rounding using a number line

units.title: Fractions as Numbers
units.summary: Fractions name equal parts and live on the number line.
objectives: Explain that a fraction names equal parts of a whole
Place simple fractions on a number line between 0 and 1
masteryCriteria: Names fractions of shapes and sets with denominators up to 12
Places unit fractions correctly on a 0–1 number line
Explains why parts must be equal

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Equal Parts
objectives: Explain that a fraction names equal parts of a whole
Place simple fractions on a number line between 0 and 1
prerequisites: Can divide a shape or set into halves
explanation: A fraction describes equal parts of a whole. The bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts the whole is split into. The top number (numerator) tells how many parts we are talking about.
The parts must be equal. Cutting a roti into three pieces of different sizes does not make thirds.
Fractions are numbers too. On a number line from 0 to 1, ½ sits exactly halfway. ¼ is halfway between 0 and ½. More equal parts means each part is smaller, so ⅛ < ¼.

vocabulary.meaning: a number naming equal parts of a whole
top number: how many parts we have
bottom number: how many equal parts in the whole
a fraction with numerator 1

examples: A pizza cut into 8 equal slices; you eat 3, so you ate ⅜.
Half of 12 marbles is 6 marbles.

story.title: The Unfair Cake
story.text: Three friends shared a cake. Momo cut it, but one piece was huge and two were tiny. "Each of us gets a third!" said Momo. "Those aren't thirds," said Nova, "thirds must be equal." They cut a new cake into three matching pieces — now each really was one third.

activities.prompt: A shape is cut into 4 EQUAL parts and 1 is coloured. What fraction is coloured?
Cutting a roti into 3 pieces of different sizes makes thirds.
activities.why: Thirds must be three equal parts.

thinking: Would you rather have ⅓ or ¼ of the same pizza? Why?
Can ½ of one thing be bigger than ½ of another? Give an example.
speaking: Fold a paper strip into halves, quarters and eighths, and explain to someone why ⅛ is smaller than ¼.

project.title: Fraction Wall
steps: Keep one strip whole and label it 1
Fold and cut strips into halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, eighths
Stack them under the whole strip
Use the wall to find which fractions are equal (like 2/4 and 1/2)
project.safety: Use child-safe scissors with adult supervision. Adults should handle sharp cutting tools and keep small paper pieces away from younger children.

assessment.prompt: A bar is split into 6 equal parts; 5 are shaded. Fraction shaded?

mastery: Names fractions of shapes and sets with denominators up to 12
Places unit fractions correctly on a 0–1 number line
Explains why parts must be equal

lessons.title: Fractions, Decimals, Percentages
objectives: Convert between simple fractions, decimals and percentages
Compare quantities given in different forms
prerequisites: Understands fractions and place value to thousandths
explanation: Decimals extend place value to the right of the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. 0.7 means 7 tenths; 0.07 means 7 hundredths.
Percent means "per hundred". 35% means 35 out of every 100, which is 0.35 or 35/100. Percentages make it easy to compare amounts out of different totals.
Key equivalents are worth memorising: ½ = 0.5 = 50%, ¼ = 0.25 = 25%, ¾ = 0.75 = 75%, ⅕ = 0.2 = 20%, 1/10 = 0.1 = 10%.

vocabulary.meaning: the dot separating whole numbers from parts
per hundred
equal in value though written differently
one of ten equal parts

examples: A test score of 18/20 is 90%.
A shirt with 25% off costs ¾ of the original price.

story.title: Which Team Shoots Better?
story.text: Team A scored 12 goals from 20 shots. Team B scored 15 from 30. "Team B scored more!" said Kiko. Nova converted: 12/20 = 60%, 15/30 = 50%. "Team A is more accurate," said Nova, "even though Team B scored more goals."

thinking: Why might a shop say "50% off" instead of "half price"? Are they the same?
Can a percentage be more than 100%? Find a real example.
speaking: Explain to someone why 0.3 is bigger than 0.25 even though 25 is bigger than 3.

project.title: Survey and Percentages

steps: Ask a question with a few choices (e.g. favourite fruit)
Tally the results
Convert each count to a fraction, decimal and percentage of the total
Present a poster with your findings
project.safety: Ask permission before surveying people. Keep answers anonymous, avoid personal or sensitive questions, and report only combined totals.

mastery: Converts fluently among fractions, decimals and percentages for common values
Compares mixed representations correctly
Explains common misconceptions such as 0.25 > 0.3

units.summary: Numbers below zero and the building blocks of whole numbers.
objectives: Identify prime and composite numbers to 100
Write a number as a product of prime factors
masteryCriteria: Identifies primes to 100 and justifies using factors

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Primes: Building Blocks of Numbers
objectives: Identify prime and composite numbers to 100
Write a number as a product of prime factors
explanation: A factor of a number divides it exactly. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13 are primes.
A composite number has more than two factors. 1 is neither prime nor composite, because it has only one factor.
Every whole number greater than 1 can be built by multiplying primes in exactly one way (ignoring order): 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Mathematicians call this the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

context.text: The "sieve" method for finding primes is credited to Eratosthenes of Cyrene, a Greek scholar of the 3rd century BCE; Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BCE) contains a proof that there are infinitely many primes.

vocabulary.meaning: a number that divides another exactly
the result of multiplying a number by a whole number
a number with exactly two factors
a number with more than two factors

examples: Negative numbers: −5 °C is colder than −2 °C.

story.title: The Rectangle Test
story.text: Bolt had 13 square tiles and wanted to make a rectangle that was not a single row. Every attempt left tiles over. With 12 tiles Bolt made 2 × 6, 3 × 4 and 1 × 12. "13 only makes one long row," Bolt said. "That is what prime means!"

activities.why: A prime has exactly two factors; 1 has only one.

activities.prompt: Match each number to its prime factorisation

thinking: Why is 2 the only even prime?
Do you think there is a largest prime number? What would that mean?
speaking: Explain the "rectangle test" for primes to someone using tiles or a drawing.

project.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
steps: Cross out 1
Circle 2 and cross out its other multiples
Repeat with the next uncrossed number (3, 5, 7)
List the circled primes and count them
Explain why you only needed to sieve up to 10

assessment.prompt: How many primes are less than 10?

mastery: Identifies primes to 100 and justifies using factors
Finds prime factorisations of numbers to 200
Orders and compares negative numbers in context

lessons.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers
objectives: Classify numbers into natural, integer, rational and irrational
Explain why √2 cannot be written as a fraction
prerequisites: Works confidently with fractions, decimals and square roots
explanation: Natural numbers (1, 2, 3, …) are for counting. Integers add zero and the negatives. Rational numbers are any number that can be written as a fraction a/b of integers with b ≠ 0 — every terminating or recurring decimal is rational.
Irrational numbers cannot be written as such a fraction. Their decimals go on forever without repeating. √2 and π are classic examples.
A proof by contradiction shows √2 is irrational: assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms; then a² = 2b², so a is even; writing a = 2k gives b² = 2k², so b is even too — contradicting "lowest terms".

context.text: Greek mathematicians knew of incommensurable lengths (such as the diagonal of a unit square) by around the 5th–4th century BCE; the popular story that a Pythagorean was drowned for revealing this is a later legend with no reliable evidence.

vocabulary.meaning: a number expressible as a fraction of integers
a real number that is not rational
a whole number, positive, negative or zero
showing an assumption leads to something impossible

examples: 0.333… = ⅓ is rational.
π ≈ 3.14159… is irrational; 22/7 is only an approximation.

story.title: The Unmeasurable Diagonal
story.text: A student drew a square with sides of 1 metre and tried to measure the diagonal exactly in centimetres, then millimetres, then smaller units. No unit ever fitted both the side and the diagonal a whole number of times. Her teacher explained: the diagonal is √2 metres, and no fraction can describe it exactly.

activities.why: 22/7 = 3.142857…, close to but not equal to π.

thinking: If √2 is irrational, what about 2√2 or √2 + 1? Can you justify your answer?
Is the sum of two irrational numbers always irrational? Look for a counterexample.

lessons.title: Standard Form
objectives: Write numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10
Use index laws including negative powers
prerequisites: Understands place value and powers of 10
explanation: Standard form writes a number as A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer. 3,800,000 = 3.8 × 10⁶ and 0.00052 = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴.
Index laws: 10ᵃ × 10ᵇ = 10ᵃ⁺ᵇ, 10ᵃ ÷ 10ᵇ = 10ᵃ⁻ᵇ, and 10⁰ = 1. A negative index means a reciprocal: 10⁻³ = 1/1000.
Scientists use standard form because it shows the size (the power) and precision (the digits of A) at a glance.

context.text: The average Earth–Sun distance is about 1.496 × 10⁸ km; a typical red blood cell is about 7–8 × 10⁻⁶ m across.

A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10

story.title: The Astronomer's Notebook
story.text: An astronomy club tried to write the distance to the nearest star beyond the Sun, about 40,000,000,000,000 km, in full on the board. They kept losing count of zeros. Writing 4.0 × 10¹³ km fitted on one line — and they could see instantly it was about 270,000 times the Earth–Sun distance.
